sermons.title: Peace in the Storm
sermons.summary: Peace is found in Christ’s presence, not the absence of storms.
sermons.reflectionPrompt: What fear are you ready to surrender?
segments: Good morning, church. Go ahead and open with me to Mark chapter 4, starting in verse 35.
It's evening. Jesus has been teaching all day, and he says to his friends, let's go over to the other side.
So they push off, and somewhere in the middle of that lake, a storm comes down on them. The waves are breaking into the boat. It's filling with water.
And here's the detail I love. Jesus is in the back of the boat, asleep on a cushion.
The disciples wake him up, and they ask the question a lot of us have asked. Teacher, don't you care that we're drowning?
Notice that the storm came while they were doing exactly what Jesus asked them to do. Obedience did not exempt them from the wind.
Some of you came in this morning thinking, if I were really following God, this wouldn't be so hard. But the boat was his idea.
Jesus gets up, and he speaks to the wind and the sea. Peace. Be still. And the wind stops, and there is a great calm.
Then he turns to them and asks, why are you so afraid? Do you still have no faith?
He isn't shaming them. He's showing them that the one who was asleep in the boat was never in danger of losing them.
Here's the big idea this morning. Peace is not the absence of the storm. Peace is the presence of Jesus in the boat.
Psalm 46 says, be still, and know that I am God. Stillness isn't pretending the waves aren't real. It's remembering who is with you in them.
So this week, when the wind picks up, I want you to try something simple. Say his name before you say your fear.
Let's pray.

takeaways.text: The storm arrived while the disciples were doing what Jesus asked. Obedience does not exempt anyone from hardship.
Peace is described as Jesus’ presence in the boat, not the absence of the storm.
A practice for the week: say his name before you say your fear.

sampleMoments.note: Obedience didn’t exempt them. Needed this.

sampleNotes: Thinking about the move to Seattle. “The boat was his idea” — I keep coming back to that.

sermons.title: When Faith Gets Loud
sermons.summary: A transformed life becomes a visible act of worship.
sermons.reflectionPrompt: Where is faith asking you to be seen?
segments: Alright, Mosaic. We are in Romans chapter 12 this morning, verses 1 and 2.
Paul has just spent eleven chapters on what God has done. And now he turns the corner with one small word. Therefore.
Therefore, in view of God's mercy, offer your bodies as a living sacrifice. That is your true and proper worship.
I want you to hear how physical that is. Not your thoughts. Not your playlist. Your body. Your Tuesday. Your hands and your calendar.
Worship was never meant to stay inside these walls. It is supposed to get loud in the places where you actually live.
And then verse 2. Do not be conformed to the pattern of this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind.
Conformed is what happens when you are pressed into a shape by the pressure around you. Like clay in a mold.
Transformed is a different word. It's the word for metamorphosis. It works from the inside out.
So the question isn't, how do I look different? It's, what is God renewing in how I think?
Loud faith is not about volume. Some of the loudest faith I've ever seen was quiet. A nurse who prays on her break. A kid who sits with the new student at lunch.
It's loud because it's visible. It costs something. It can be seen.
Here's the big idea. A transformed life becomes a visible act of worship.
So where is faith asking you to be seen this week? Not to be impressive. Just to be honest about who you belong to.
Let's stand and respond together.

takeaways.text: Paul grounds the call to worship in God’s mercy before asking anything of the listener.
Being conformed comes from outside pressure; being transformed works from the inside out through a renewed mind.
Loud faith is described as visible and costly rather than high-volume.

sampleMoments.note: The nurse who prays on her break

sampleNotes: Ask Dani about the Tuesday night thing at the shelter.

sermons.title: Open Hands
sermons.summary: Trust loosens our grip on what tomorrow might bring.
sermons.reflectionPrompt: What are you holding too tightly?
segments: Hey, Citylight. If you've got a Bible, turn to Matthew chapter 6. We're picking up in verse 25.
Jesus says, therefore I tell you, do not worry about your life, what you will eat or drink, or about your body, what you will wear.
Now, I'll be honest. When I read that, my first reaction is, easy for you to say. Rent is due on the first.
But Jesus doesn't say this from a distance. He says it to people who lived one bad harvest away from hunger.
Look at the birds of the air, he says. They don't sow or reap or store in barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them.
Consider the lilies of the field. They don't labor or spin. And not even Solomon in all his splendor was dressed like one of these.
Worry is what happens when we try to hold tomorrow in hands that were made for today.
Can any one of you, by worrying, add a single hour to your life? The honest answer is no. It usually takes a few.
So Jesus gives us a different posture. Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be given to you as well.
Seek first doesn't mean seek only. It means order. It means God gets the first grip, and we hold everything else a little more loosely.
I've started praying with my hands open. Literally. Palms up. It feels a little awkward. It's supposed to.
Here's the big idea. Trust loosens our grip on what tomorrow might bring.
Do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will worry about itself. Each day has enough trouble of its own.
So what are you holding too tightly right now? Let's bring it to him.

takeaways.text: Jesus spoke about worry to people with real material insecurity, not from a distance.
Seeking the kingdom first is framed as an order of priorities, not a call to ignore daily needs.
A suggested practice: praying with open hands as a physical sign of trust.

sampleNotes: Try the palms-up prayer before work this week.

sermons.title: Built in the Waiting
sermons.summary: Waiting is not wasted when it is shaping who we become.
sermons.reflectionPrompt: What could God be forming in this pause?
segments: Good morning. We're spending some time today in Psalm 27, a psalm of David.
It opens with confidence. The Lord is my light and my salvation. Whom shall I fear?
But if you keep reading, the tone changes. Hear me, Lord, when I call. Do not hide your face from me.
In the same song, David moves from certainty to longing. And I find that strangely comforting.
Because most of us live in the middle of that psalm. We believe, and we're still waiting.
Waiting on a diagnosis. Waiting on a job. Waiting for a prodigal to come home. Waiting for the grief to lift.
We usually treat waiting like a hallway. Something to rush through on the way to the room where life happens.
But in scripture, the waiting is often the room. It's where God does some of his most patient work.
David says, one thing I ask of the Lord, this is what I seek. That I may dwell in the house of the Lord and gaze on his beauty.
In the waiting, his request got smaller and deeper at the same time. Not ten things. One thing.
And then the last verse. Wait for the Lord. Be strong and take heart, and wait for the Lord.
He says it twice. Maybe because he knew we'd need to hear it twice.
Here's the big idea. Waiting is not wasted when it is shaping who we become.
So let me ask you. What could God be forming in you, in this pause?

takeaways.text: Psalm 27 holds confidence and longing together, which mirrors believing while still waiting.
Waiting is presented as a place where God works, not just a hallway to pass through.
In waiting, David’s request narrows to one thing: to dwell with God and see his beauty.

sampleNotes: Mom’s appointment is Thursday. One thing.

sermons.title: The Table Gets Wider
sermons.summary: Grace keeps making room for people we did not expect.
sermons.reflectionPrompt: Who might need an invitation from you?
segments: Common Ground, good morning. Let's go to Luke chapter 14, verse 15.
Jesus is at a dinner party at the house of a prominent religious leader. Everyone is watching where everyone sits.
And someone at the table says, blessed is the one who will eat at the feast in the kingdom of God. It's a nice thing to say at dinner.
So Jesus tells a story. A man is preparing a great banquet, and he invites many guests.
But when the food is ready, the excuses start. I just bought a field. I just bought five yoke of oxen. I just got married.
Every excuse is reasonable. That's what makes them dangerous. None of them are bad things. They're just more important things.
So the master says to his servant, go out quickly into the streets and alleys of the town, and bring in the poor, the crippled, the blind, and the lame.
And the servant comes back and says, it's done. And there is still room.
Church, I want that sentence over our doors. There is still room.
Then go out to the roads and the country lanes, and compel them to come in, so that my house will be full.
The table in this story doesn't get more exclusive. It keeps getting wider.
Here's the big idea. Grace keeps making room for people we did not expect.
And if grace made room for us, then our tables, our group chats, our Sunday lunches, can get a little wider too.
Who might need an invitation from you this week?

takeaways.text: The guests’ excuses were reasonable, which is what made them easy to accept.
The master’s response to refusal is to widen the invitation, not shrink the feast.
An application: let ordinary tables — meals, group chats, Sunday lunch — get wider.

sampleNotes: Invite the new neighbors for Sunday lunch.

sermons.title: Start Where You Are
sermons.summary: Faith becomes tangible through the next faithful action.
sermons.reflectionPrompt: What is one good thing you can begin today?
segments: Morning, Anchor. Grab your Bible and meet me in James chapter 2, verse 14.
James is the brother of Jesus, and he writes like a big brother. Short sentences. No wasted words.
What good is it, my brothers and sisters, if someone claims to have faith but has no deeds? Can such faith save them?
Then he gives an example that's almost uncomfortable. Someone is without clothes and daily food.
And you say to them, go in peace, keep warm and well fed. But you do nothing about their physical needs. What good is it?
I've said go in peace. I've said I'll be praying for you, and meant it, and then gone home and done nothing else.
James isn't saying we earn grace by good works. He's saying living faith moves. It has a pulse.
In the same way, faith by itself, if it is not accompanied by action, is dead.
And here's what I think keeps a lot of us stuck. We wait until we can do something big.
We want to fix the whole problem, so we don't touch any part of it.
But James never asks for the whole problem. He asks about the person in front of you. Clothes. Food. Today.
Show me your faith without deeds, he says, and I will show you my faith by my deeds.
Here's the big idea. Faith becomes tangible through the next faithful action. Not the biggest one. The next one.
So what is one good thing you can begin today? Start where you are.

outline.title: Go in peace, and do nothing?

takeaways.text: James distinguishes earning grace from living faith: genuine faith shows up in action.
Waiting to do something big can keep people from doing anything at all.
James focuses on the person in front of you and their immediate needs.

sampleNotes: Drop off the coats at the shelter on Saturday.

sermons.title: Songs in the Night
sermons.summary: Worship in the dark declares who God is before we see what he will do.
sermons.reflectionPrompt: What song do you need to sing before morning?
segments: Good evening, Harbor and Vine. Turn with me to Acts chapter 16. We'll start at verse 25.
Paul and Silas have been beaten with rods and thrown into the inner cell of a prison. Their feet are fastened in stocks.
And the text says, about midnight, Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the other prisoners were listening to them.
I want you to sit with that. It's midnight. Nothing has changed yet. And they are singing.
We tend to think worship is the response to the rescue. Here, worship comes before anything moves.
And the other prisoners were listening. Your song in the night is never only for you. Someone in the next cell is listening.
Suddenly there was a great earthquake. The foundations were shaken, every door flew open, and everyone's chains came loose.
The jailer wakes up, sees the doors open, and assumes the worst. He draws his sword.
And Paul shouts, don't harm yourself. We are all here.
Think about that. The doors are open, and they stay. Because the jailer mattered more than the exit.
The jailer asks, what must I do to be saved? And that night, his whole household is baptized, and he sets a meal before them, filled with joy.
The night that began in chains ends at a kitchen table.
Here's the big idea. Worship in the dark is not denial. It's declaring who God is before you can see what he'll do.
So what song do you need to sing before morning comes?

outline.title: From chains to a kitchen table

takeaways.text: In this passage, worship happens before circumstances change, not only after rescue.
Worship in hard seasons has an audience: others are listening.
Paul and Silas stay when the doors open because the jailer’s life mattered more than escape.

sampleMoments.note: Someone in the next cell is listening.

sermons.title: Breakfast on the Shore
sermons.summary: Jesus restores us where we failed, then hands us something to carry.
sermons.reflectionPrompt: Where might he be building a fire for you?
segments: Riverside, good morning. We're in John chapter 21, the last chapter of the gospel.
After the resurrection, Peter tells the others, I'm going fishing. It's the most ordinary sentence in the book.
He's going back to what he knew before Jesus called him. Because after you've failed someone, the old life can feel safer.
They fish all night and catch nothing. And at dawn, a man on the shore calls out, friends, haven't you any fish?
He tells them to throw the net on the right side, and they can't haul it in because of the number of fish.
John says, it is the Lord. And Peter doesn't wait for the boat. He jumps into the water.
When they land, they see a fire of burning coals there, with fish on it, and some bread.
The last time Peter stood by a charcoal fire, he denied Jesus three times. Now Jesus has built another one.
Jesus doesn't start with a lecture. He starts with breakfast. Come and eat.
Then three times, Jesus asks him, Simon son of John, do you love me? Three questions for three denials.
And each time, Jesus gives him a job. Feed my lambs. Take care of my sheep. Feed my sheep.
Restoration in this story isn't just forgiveness. It's being trusted again.
Here's the big idea. Jesus restores us at the place of our failure, and then he hands us something to carry.
Where might he be building a fire for you, right where things went wrong?

takeaways.text: The charcoal fire echoes the scene of Peter’s denial; Jesus restores him at the place of failure.
Jesus begins with breakfast, not a lecture.
Restoration includes being trusted again: each question comes with a charge to care for others.

sampleNotes: Call Marcus. It’s been too long.
